content.intro: Learn filtering rows with where through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Filtering Rows With WHERE matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of filtering rows with where is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea

Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Filtering numeric values
items.text: Filtering numeric values works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: Filtering text values
items.text: Filtering text values depends on text representation, collation, wildcard semantics, and sometimes locale. Test spaces, case, accents, Unicode, and special characters rather than assuming every database compares strings identically.

items.title: Filtering date and time values
items.text: Filtering date and time values needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT product_id, name, price
FROM products
WHERE price >= 25 AND is_active = TRUE
ORDER BY price DESC, product_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: The query filters active products at or above the chosen price threshold, then sorts the remaining rows.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
